title: Probability and Statistics

sources.title: Imperial College London Department of Mathematics Undergraduate Programme Handbook 2026-27
sources.used_for: module description (axiomatic probability in Term 1; modelling and data analysis with packages such as R in Term 2), core status, 10 ECTS, timing, contact hours, assessment pattern and progression rule for core modules

about: Probability and Statistics (MATH40005) is a core 10-ECTS module in Year 1 of Imperial's Mathematics BSc, running from week 5 of Term 1 through Term 2 with about 40 lectures and 14 classes (2026-27 handbook). The first term develops probability within an axiomatic framework; the second term emphasises principles of modelling and data analysis, fitting and criticising statistical models on real data sets with a package such as R. Summative assessment in 2026-27 is a 1-hour exam in week 1 of Term 2 (15%), a 1-hour in-class test in week 6 of Term 2 (15%) and a 2-hour final exam in Term 3 (70%), and core modules must be passed (after resits if needed) to progress. The handbook gives no detailed syllabus, so the eight topics here are a standard first-year probability and statistics course built from that description; check the order and coverage against your lecture notes.
topics: Probability spaces: axioms, consequences and counting
Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
Discrete random variables and standard distributions
Continuous random variables and standard distributions
Joint distributions, covariance and limit theorems
Statistical models and maximum likelihood estimation
Linear regression and model checking in R

notes.body:
The autumn half of the module builds probability from axioms, so every rule you use must be derived from them. Exam questions often ask you to prove a simple property directly from the axioms.

Probability space (Ω, F, P)
- Ω is the sample space, the set of all outcomes.
- F is a σ-algebra of subsets of Ω (the events): it contains Ω, it is closed under complements, and it is closed under countable unions.
- P: F → [0, 1] is a probability measure satisfying Kolmogorov's axioms:
  1. P(A) ≥ 0 for every A in F;
  2. P(Ω) = 1;
  3. countable additivity: if A₁, A₂, … are pairwise disjoint events, then P(∪Aᵢ) = Σ P(Aᵢ).

Consequences you should be able to prove
- P(∅) = 0.
- Finite additivity for disjoint A and B.
- Complement rule: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A).
- Monotonicity: if A ⊆ B, then P(A) ≤ P(B).
- Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
- Boole's inequality: P(A₁ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ) ≤ Σ P(Aᵢ), true for any events.
- Inclusion–exclusion for three events: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣP(A) − ΣP(A ∩ B) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C).
- Continuity: if A₁ ⊆ A₂ ⊆ … then P(∪Aₙ) = lim P(Aₙ); if A₁ ⊇ A₂ ⊇ … then P(∩Aₙ) = lim P(Aₙ).

Typical proof: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Write A ∪ B as the disjoint union A ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ), and B as the disjoint union (B ∩ A) ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ). Additivity on both, then subtract.

Zero probability is not impossibility. If X is uniform on [0, 1], the event {X = ½} is non-empty but has probability 0.

Equally likely outcomes
If Ω is finite and every outcome is equally likely, P(A) = |A|/|Ω|, so probability becomes counting.
- Ordered selections without replacement: n!/(n − k)!.
- Unordered selections: C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!).
- With replacement and ordered: nᵏ.
- Example: the probability of exactly 2 heads in 5 fair tosses is C(5, 2)/2⁵ = 10/32 = 0.3125.
- Birthday problem (365 equally likely birthdays, independent): with 23 people, P(at least two share) = 1 − (365 × 364 × … × 343)/365²³ ≈ 0.507. It is usually easier to compute the complement.

Exam tips: in proofs, cite which axiom each step uses and build disjoint unions explicitly; in counting, decide first whether order matters and whether there is replacement.

Conditioning updates probabilities in the light of information. It is where most exam errors happen, usually by confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A).

Conditional probability
- For P(B) > 0: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B).
- For fixed B, P(· | B) is itself a probability measure, so all the rules from the axioms apply to it.
- Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B). Chain rule: P(A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ A₃) = P(A₁)P(A₂ | A₁)P(A₃ | A₁ ∩ A₂), when the conditioning events have positive probability.

Law of total probability
If B₁, B₂, … form a partition of Ω (pairwise disjoint, union Ω) with each P(Bᵢ) > 0, then P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).

Bayes' theorem
With the same partition and P(A) > 0: P(Bⱼ | A) = P(A | Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ) / Σᵢ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).

Worked example (screening)
A condition has prevalence 1%. A test detects it with probability 0.95 (sensitivity) and gives a false positive with probability 0.05.
- P(+) = 0.01 × 0.95 + 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.059.
- P(D | +) = 0.0095/0.059 ≈ 0.161.
- So only about 16% of positives have the condition: the many healthy people produce many false positives. This is the base-rate effect.
- After a second, conditionally independent positive test: P(D | ++) = 0.01 × 0.95² / (0.01 × 0.95² + 0.99 × 0.05²) ≈ 0.785.

Independence
- A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). This definition works even when P(B) = 0; when P(B) > 0 it is equivalent to P(A | B) = P(A).
- If A and B are independent, so are A and Bᶜ, Aᶜ and B, and Aᶜ and Bᶜ.
- Events A₁, …, Aₙ are mutually independent if P(∩ of Aᵢ, i in S) = Π P(Aᵢ) for every subset S. Pairwise independence is weaker. Example: toss two fair coins and let A = first is H, B = second is H, C = both the same. Each pair is independent, but P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = ¼ ≠ ⅛.
- Independence is not the same as being disjoint. Disjoint events with positive probability are never independent.
- Surprising example: roll two fair dice, A = first die even, B = total is 7. P(A ∩ B) = 3/36 = 1/12 = ½ × 1/6, so A and B are independent.

Conditional independence: A and B are conditionally independent given C (with P(C) > 0) if P(A ∩ B | C) = P(A | C)P(B | C). This is the assumption behind repeated tests above.

Exam tips: define your events in words, draw a tree for multi-stage problems, and state the partition when you use total probability or Bayes.

A random variable is a function X: Ω → ℝ such that {X ≤ x} is an event for every x. X is discrete if it takes values in a finite or countable set.

Describing a discrete distribution
- Probability mass function (pmf): p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1.
- Cumulative distribution function (cdf): F(x) = P(X ≤ x). It is non-decreasing and right-continuous, tends to 0 as x → −∞ and to 1 as x → +∞, and is a step function for discrete X.

Expectation and variance
- E[X] = Σ x p(x), provided Σ |x| p(x) < ∞. Otherwise the expectation does not exist.
- Law of the unconscious statistician: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) p(x), under the same absolute-convergence condition.
- Linearity: E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c, whenever E[X] and E[Y] exist, with no independence needed.
- Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])², for E[X²] < ∞.
- Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X). The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Standard distributions (q = 1 − p)
- Bernoulli(p): P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = q. Mean p, variance pq.
- Binomial(n, p): the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials. P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏq^(n−k) for k = 0, …, n. Mean np, variance npq.
- Geometric(p), counting the trials up to and including the first success: P(X = k) = q^(k−1)p for k = 1, 2, … Mean 1/p, variance q/p². It is memoryless: P(X > m + n | X > m) = P(X > n). (Some books count failures instead, which shifts the support to 0, 1, 2, … and the mean to q/p. Check the convention.)
- Poisson(λ), λ > 0: P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k! for k = 0, 1, 2, … Mean λ and variance λ.

Poisson limit of the binomial
If n → ∞ and p → 0 with np → λ, then C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)^(n−k) → e^(−λ)λᵏ/k! for each fixed k. In practice Bin(n, p) ≈ Poisson(np) when n is large and p is small.

Worked examples
- X ~ Bin(10, 0.3): E[X] = 3, Var(X) = 2.1, sd ≈ 1.449.
- Calls arrive as Poisson with mean 2 per minute. P(at least 2 in a minute) = 1 − e^(−2)(1 + 2) = 1 − 3e^(−2) ≈ 0.594.
- If Var(X) = 4, then Var(3X − 2) = 9 × 4 = 36.

Deriving moments: for the Poisson, E[X] = Σ k e^(−λ)λᵏ/k! = λ Σ e^(−λ)λ^(k−1)/(k − 1)! = λ. For the variance, compute E[X(X − 1)] = λ² first, then Var = λ² + λ − λ² = λ.

Exam tips: state the distribution and its parameters with a reason ('n independent trials with constant p'), and use the factorial-moment trick E[X(X − 1)] for binomial and Poisson variances.

X is (absolutely) continuous if there is a probability density function (pdf) f ≥ 0 with P(X ∈ [a, b]) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx for all a ≤ b, and ∫ f = 1 over ℝ.

Key facts
- P(X = x) = 0 for every x, so ≤ and < give the same probabilities.
- The cdf F(x) = ∫ from −∞ to x of f(t) dt is continuous, and F′(x) = f(x) wherever f is continuous.
- f(x) is a density, not a probability: it can exceed 1.
- E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx, provided ∫ |x| f(x) dx < ∞; E[g(X)] = ∫ g(x) f(x) dx under the same kind of condition.
- Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².

Worked example: f(x) = c x² on [0, 2], 0 elsewhere
- Normalise: c × 8/3 = 1, so c = 3/8.
- E[X] = ∫₀² x × 3x²/8 dx = 3/2.
- E[X²] = ∫₀² 3x⁴/8 dx = 12/5, so Var(X) = 12/5 − 9/4 = 3/20 = 0.15.
- P(X < 1) = (3/8)(1/3) = 1/8.

Standard distributions
- Uniform U(a, b): f = 1/(b − a) on [a, b]. Mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12.
- Exponential(λ), with rate λ > 0: f(x) = λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0. Survival P(X > x) = e^(−λx). Mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ².
  - Memoryless: for s, t ≥ 0, P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). It is the only continuous distribution with this property.
- Normal N(μ, σ²): f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) exp(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)). If X ~ N(μ, σ²) then Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1), with cdf Φ.
  - Useful values: Φ(1.645) ≈ 0.95, Φ(1.96) ≈ 0.975, Φ(2) ≈ 0.977.
  - Example: X ~ N(100, 15²). P(X > 130) = 1 − Φ(2) ≈ 0.0228.

Transformations of a random variable
- Distribution-function method: find F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y) directly, then differentiate.
- Change-of-variable formula: if X has pdf f_X, and g is strictly monotone and differentiable on the range of X with differentiable inverse, then Y = g(X) has pdf f_Y(y) = f_X(g⁻¹(y)) |d g⁻¹(y)/dy| on the range of g.
- Example: U ~ U(0, 1) and Y = −(1/λ) ln U. Then P(Y > y) = P(U < e^(−λy)) = e^(−λy), so Y ~ Exp(λ). This is the inverse-transform method used to simulate random variables.
- Non-monotone g (e.g. Y = X²): use the cdf method and add up the contributions from each branch.

Exam tips: always check that a proposed pdf integrates to 1, state the support of transformed variables, and standardise normal variables before using tables.

notes.h: Several random variables, sums and limit theorems
notes.body:
Joint distributions
- Discrete: joint pmf p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y). The marginals are p_X(x) = Σ_y p(x, y), and similarly for Y.
- Continuous: joint pdf f(x, y), with P((X, Y) ∈ A) = ∫∫_A f dx dy and marginal f_X(x) = ∫ f(x, y) dy.
- X and Y are independent if and only if the joint pmf or pdf factorises as a product of the marginals, for all x and y.
- Conditional pmf: p(x | y) = p(x, y)/p_Y(y) when p_Y(y) > 0.

Covariance and correlation (assuming finite second moments)
- Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y].
- Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2Cov(X, Y). More generally, Var(ΣXᵢ) = ΣVar Xᵢ + 2Σ over i<j of Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ).
- Correlation ρ = Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) lies in [−1, 1]. |ρ| = 1 exactly when Y is (almost surely) a linear function of X.
- Independent implies uncorrelated. The converse is false. Example: X ~ U(−1, 1) and Y = X². Then Cov(X, Y) = E[X³] − 0 = 0, but Y is determined by X: for example P(Y < ¼) = ½, while P(Y < ¼ | X > ½) = 0.

Sums of independent random variables
- Means always add; variances add when the variables are independent (or just uncorrelated).
- Sums of independent binomials Bin(m, p) + Bin(n, p) = Bin(m + n, p) (same p); independent Poissons add their means; independent normals give N(μ₁ + μ₂, σ₁² + σ₂²).
- The sample mean X̄ of n iid variables with mean μ and variance σ² has E[X̄] = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n.

Inequalities
- Markov: if X ≥ 0 and a > 0, then P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a.
- Chebyshev: if Var X = σ² < ∞ and k > 0, then P(|X − μ| ≥ k) ≤ σ²/k². For k = 2σ the bound is ¼, whereas a normal gives about 0.046. Chebyshev holds for every distribution with finite variance, which is why it is weaker.

Limit theorems (X₁, X₂, … iid)
- Weak law of large numbers: if E|X₁| < ∞ with mean μ, then for every ε > 0, P(|X̄ₙ − μ| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞. With finite variance it follows directly from Chebyshev: P(|X̄ₙ − μ| > ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²).
- Central limit theorem: if the mean is μ and the variance σ² is finite with 0 < σ², then for every z, P((X̄ₙ − μ)/(σ/√n) ≤ z) → Φ(z). Equivalently Σ Xᵢ ≈ N(nμ, nσ²) for large n.

Worked CLT example
100 iid variables with mean 5 and variance 4. The sum S has mean 500 and standard deviation √(100 × 4) = 20. So P(S > 520) ≈ 1 − Φ(1) ≈ 0.159.

Exam tips: state independence and identical distribution explicitly before using the CLT, and remember that the standard deviation of a sum grows like √n, not n.

From the spring term the module turns from probability to statistics: using data to learn about an unknown model. The handbook stresses modelling principles and criticising models, not just computing estimates.

Parametric models
- A statistical model treats the data x₁, …, xₙ as observed values of random variables X₁, …, Xₙ with a distribution known up to a parameter θ. For example: 'the Xᵢ are iid Poisson(λ)'.
- Modelling choices (independence, identical distribution, family) should be justified from the context and then checked against the data.

Estimators
- An estimator θ̂ = T(X₁, …, Xₙ) is a random variable; its value on the data is an estimate.
- Bias: E[θ̂] − θ. θ̂ is unbiased if the bias is 0 for all θ.
- Mean squared error: MSE = E[(θ̂ − θ)²] = Var(θ̂) + bias². A slightly biased estimator can have smaller MSE.
- Consistency: θ̂ₙ → θ in probability as n → ∞.
- The standard error is the standard deviation of θ̂ (or an estimate of it).

Maximum likelihood
- Likelihood: L(θ) = Π f(xᵢ; θ) (pmf or pdf) for iid data, viewed as a function of θ. The log-likelihood is ℓ(θ) = Σ log f(xᵢ; θ).
- The MLE θ̂ maximises L, equivalently ℓ. Usually you solve ℓ′(θ) = 0 and check ℓ″ < 0. Watch out for boundary maxima, e.g. U(0, θ), where the MLE is max xᵢ.
- Invariance: the MLE of g(θ) is g(θ̂).

Standard MLEs (iid samples)
- Bernoulli(p): p̂ = x̄.
- Poisson(λ): ℓ(λ) = −nλ + (Σxᵢ) log λ − Σ log xᵢ!. Setting ℓ′ = −n + Σxᵢ/λ = 0 gives λ̂ = x̄, and ℓ″ = −Σxᵢ/λ² < 0 when Σxᵢ > 0. Data 2, 3, 1, 4, 0 give λ̂ = 2.
- Exponential with rate λ: λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 1/x̄. With n = 10 and Σxᵢ = 40, λ̂ = 0.25.
- Normal N(μ, σ²): μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − x̄)².

Bias of the normal variance MLE
E[Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²] = (n − 1)σ², so E[σ̂²] = (n − 1)σ²/n, which is biased low. The sample variance S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1) is unbiased. This is why software reports S² by default.

Method of moments
Set the sample moments equal to the theoretical ones and solve. For the Poisson and exponential this gives the same answers as maximum likelihood.

Exploratory analysis first
Before fitting, look at the data: summary statistics, histograms, boxplots and scatterplots. They show outliers, skewness and whether a proposed family is plausible. For a Poisson model, compare the sample mean and variance; a variance much larger than the mean (overdispersion) suggests the model is wrong.

Exam tips: write the likelihood, take logs, differentiate, solve, and check it is a maximum; state any condition, such as Σxᵢ > 0.

Point estimates need a measure of uncertainty. Confidence intervals and tests both use the sampling distribution of an estimator.

Key sampling results for normal data (X₁, …, Xₙ iid N(μ, σ²))
- X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n).
- (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) has a t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, where S² is the sample variance with divisor n − 1. The t distribution has heavier tails than N(0, 1) and approaches it as n grows.

Confidence intervals
- σ known: x̄ ± z_(α/2) σ/√n, with z₀.₀₂₅ = 1.96 for 95%.
- σ unknown: x̄ ± t_(n−1, α/2) s/√n.
- Large samples, any distribution with finite variance: the CLT gives an approximate interval x̄ ± 1.96 × (estimated standard error).
- Interpretation: the interval is random and μ is fixed. If the procedure were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain μ. It is not correct to say that μ has a 95% probability of lying in the particular interval you computed.
- Worked example: n = 16, x̄ = 52, s = 4. Then t₁₅,₀.₀₂₅ ≈ 2.131 and the standard error is 4/4 = 1, so the 95% CI is 52 ± 2.131 = (49.87, 54.13).

Hypothesis tests
- Null hypothesis H₀ (e.g. μ = 50) and alternative H₁ (e.g. μ ≠ 50).
- The test statistic measures departure from H₀. Here T = (X̄ − 50)/(S/√n), which has a t₁₅ distribution under H₀. The observed value is (52 − 50)/1 = 2.0.
- p-value: the probability, computed assuming H₀ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. Here p = P(|t₁₅| ≥ 2.0) ≈ 0.064.
- Decision at significance level α: reject H₀ if p ≤ α. Here p > 0.05, so we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level, although there is some weak evidence against it. Consistently, 50 lies inside the 95% CI. For the one-sample t-test and the matching t-interval (and in general whenever the interval is built by inverting the test), a two-sided test at level α rejects exactly when the 100(1 − α)% interval excludes the null value. Approximate tests and intervals that use different standard errors need not agree exactly near the boundary.

Errors and power
- Type I error: rejecting a true H₀. Its probability is the size α.
- Type II error: failing to reject a false H₀.
- Power = 1 − P(type II error). It increases with sample size and with the size of the true effect.
- 'Not rejecting H₀' is not evidence that H₀ is true, especially with a small sample.

Other common tests
- Two-sample t-test (independent groups, often assuming equal variances) and the paired t-test (differences within pairs).
- Approximate z-test for a proportion: z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n).
- Goodness of fit: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, compared with a χ² distribution. Expected counts should not be too small.

Exam tips: always state H₀, H₁, the test statistic and its null distribution, the p-value and a conclusion in context; and check the assumptions (independence, approximate normality).

notes.h: Simple linear regression and model criticism
notes.body:
The spring term uses real data sets and a statistical package such as R to fit and criticise models. Simple linear regression is the standard first model for the relationship between two variables.

The model
- Yᵢ = β₀ + β₁xᵢ + εᵢ for i = 1, …, n, with εᵢ iid N(0, σ²). The xᵢ are treated as fixed.
- Assumptions to check: linearity, independence, constant variance (homoscedasticity) and normality of the errors.

Least squares
- Choose β₀ and β₁ to minimise Σ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ)². Under the normal-errors model these are also the MLEs.
- With S_xx = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² and S_xy = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ): β̂₁ = S_xy/S_xx and β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄. The fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
- Residuals eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ sum to zero. RSS = Σeᵢ², and σ̂² = RSS/(n − 2) estimates σ² (two parameters were estimated).
- R² = 1 − RSS/S_yy is the proportion of variation explained. In simple regression it equals r², the squared sample correlation.

Worked example
x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 1, 3, 2, 5, 4.
- x̄ = ȳ = 3, S_xx = 10, S_xy = 8, S_yy = 10.
- β̂₁ = 0.8 and β̂₀ = 3 − 2.4 = 0.6, so ŷ = 0.6 + 0.8x.
- Residuals: −0.4, 0.8, −1.0, 1.2, −0.6. RSS = 3.6 and R² = 1 − 3.6/10 = 0.64.
- σ̂² = 3.6/3 = 1.2. SE(β̂₁) = √(σ̂²/S_xx) ≈ 0.346, so t = 0.8/0.346 ≈ 2.31 on 3 df, and p ≈ 0.10 for H₀: β₁ = 0.
- With only five points, the evidence for a non-zero slope is weak, despite R² = 0.64.

Inference on the slope: (β̂₁ − β₁)/SE(β̂₁) ~ t with n − 2 df, which gives tests and intervals for β₁.

Criticising the model (diagnostics)
- Residuals against fitted values: should be a patternless band. A curve suggests non-linearity; a funnel suggests non-constant variance (try a transformation such as log y).
- Normal QQ plot of the residuals: points close to a straight line support normal errors. Systematic bends suggest skewness or heavy tails.
- Look for outliers and for influential points. A point with high leverage (an extreme x value) can pull the line, especially if it also has a large residual; check by refitting without it.
- Residuals plotted in time order can reveal dependence.
- Correlation is not causation, and predictions far outside the range of the data (extrapolation) are unreliable.

Using R
In R, a linear model is fitted with lm() using a formula such as y ~ x. summary() reports the estimates, standard errors, t-values, p-values and R², and plot() applied to the fitted model produces the standard diagnostic plots. Practise reading this output: exams often show output and ask you to interpret it.

Exam tips: quote the fitted equation with units, interpret the slope in context ('each extra unit of x is associated with…'), and justify the assumptions using the residual plots.

cards.b: P(A) ≥ 0; P(Ω) = 1; for pairwise disjoint A₁, A₂, …, P(∪Aᵢ) = ΣP(Aᵢ) (countable additivity).
A collection of subsets containing Ω, closed under complements and under countable unions.
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), for any events A, B.
P(A₁ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ) ≤ P(A₁) + … + P(Aₙ), for any events (disjoint or not).
If A₁ ⊆ A₂ ⊆ …, then P(∪Aₙ) = lim P(Aₙ).
No. For X uniform on [0, 1], {X = ½} is non-empty but has probability 0.
P(at least two share a birthday) ≈ 0.507, assuming 365 equally likely, independent birthdays.
P(A ∩ B)/P(B), defined when P(B) > 0.
For a partition B₁, B₂, … of Ω with each P(Bᵢ) > 0: P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
P(Bⱼ | A) = P(A | Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ) / Σᵢ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ), for a partition with P(Bᵢ) > 0 and P(A) > 0.
P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
The product rule holds for every subset of the events, not just for pairs.

cards.f: Pairwise but not mutually independent: example
cards.b: Two fair coins; A = first H, B = second H, C = both the same. Each pair is independent, but P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = ¼ ≠ ⅛.
With a rare condition, even an accurate test gives a low P(condition | positive), because false positives from the large healthy group dominate.
E[X] = Σ x p(x), defined only if Σ|x| p(x) < ∞.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.8. What is the probability that exactly one of A and B occurs?
questions.why: The addition rule gives P(A ∩ B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.8 = 0.3, so P(exactly one) = P(A ∪ B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.8 − 0.3 = 0.5. 0.8 is the probability of at least one, which you get by subtracting the overlap only once (from P(A) + P(B)) rather than twice. 0.3 is the probability that both occur. 0.2 is P(neither) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).

questions.q: Which statement follows from Kolmogorov's axioms for all events A and B?
options: If A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability, they are independent
questions.why: Boole's inequality holds for all events, since P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) and P(A ∩ B) ≥ 0. Equality of P(A ∪ B) with P(A) + P(B) needs A and B to be disjoint (or to overlap with probability 0). A probability-zero event can be non-empty, e.g. a single point under a continuous uniform distribution. Disjoint events with positive probabilities are dependent: P(A ∩ B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0.

questions.q: Using only Kolmogorov's axioms (and finite additivity, which follows from them), prove that P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) and that A ⊆ B implies P(A) ≤ P(B).
markScheme: Ω = A ∪ Aᶜ with A and Aᶜ disjoint
Additivity and P(Ω) = 1 give P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = 1
For A ⊆ B, write B = A ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ), a disjoint union
P(B) = P(A) + P(B ∩ Aᶜ) ≥ P(A), since P(B ∩ Aᶜ) ≥ 0 by the first axiom
questions.modelAnswer: A and Aᶜ are disjoint and their union is Ω. By additivity and the second axiom, 1 = P(Ω) = P(A) + P(Aᶜ), so P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A). If A ⊆ B, then B = A ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ), and these two sets are disjoint. So P(B) = P(A) + P(B ∩ Aᶜ). By the first axiom P(B ∩ Aᶜ) ≥ 0, hence P(B) ≥ P(A).

questions.q: A condition has prevalence 1%. A test is positive with probability 0.95 if the condition is present and 0.05 if it is absent. Given a positive result, what is the probability that the condition is present?
questions.why: By Bayes, P(D | +) = 0.01 × 0.95/(0.01 × 0.95 + 0.99 × 0.05) = 0.0095/0.059 ≈ 0.161. 0.95 is P(+ | D), the sensitivity; giving it is the classic error of reversing the conditioning. 0.01 is the prior, which ignores the test result. 0.0095 is the joint probability P(D ∩ +), before dividing by P(+).

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. A = the first die shows an even number; B = the total is 7. Which statement is correct?
options: A and B are dependent, because the total depends on the first die
A and B are mutually exclusive
questions.why: P(A) = ½ and P(B) = 6/36 = 1/6. A ∩ B = {(2, 5), (4, 3), (6, 1)}, so P(A ∩ B) = 3/36 = 1/12 = P(A)P(B): independent. The intuition that the total depends on the first die is true in general, but independence is defined by the product rule, and here it holds. They are not mutually exclusive, since (2, 5) lies in both. P(A ∩ B) = 1/6 is P(B), from counting all six outcomes with total 7 instead of only those with an even first die.

questions.q: For the test in the screening example (prevalence 1%, sensitivity 0.95, false positive rate 0.05), a person tests positive twice. Assuming the two results are conditionally independent given disease status, find P(condition | two positives).
markScheme: P(++ | D) = 0.95² = 0.9025 and P(++ | Dᶜ) = 0.05² = 0.0025, using conditional independence
Comment: a second positive raises the probability from about 0.16 to about 0.78
questions.modelAnswer: By conditional independence, P(++ | D) = 0.95² = 0.9025 and P(++ | Dᶜ) = 0.05² = 0.0025. By total probability, P(++) = 0.01 × 0.9025 + 0.99 × 0.0025 = 0.009025 + 0.002475 = 0.0115. By Bayes, P(D | ++) = 0.009025/0.0115 ≈ 0.785. The second positive raises the probability from about 0.16 to about 0.78. Equivalently, the posterior after one test (0.161) becomes the prior for the second.

questions.q: X ~ Bin(10, 0.3). What is Var(X)?
questions.why: Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1. 3 is the mean np. 0.21 is p(1 − p), the variance of a single Bernoulli trial, missing the factor n. 1.449 is √2.1, the standard deviation, not the variance.

questions.q: Var(X) = 4. What is Var(3X − 2)?
questions.why: Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) = 9 × 4 = 36; the constant −2 shifts X but does not change its spread. 12 multiplies by a = 3 instead of a² = 9. 34 squares correctly but then wrongly subtracts the constant 2. 10 multiplies by 3 and subtracts 2, treating variance as if it were linear like expectation.

questions.q: Phone calls arrive at a desk according to a Poisson distribution with mean 2 per minute. (a) Find the probability of at least 2 calls in a given minute. (b) Explain why the number of calls in a 3-minute period has mean 6 and variance 6, stating the assumption you need.
markScheme: Assume counts in disjoint minutes are independent Poisson(2)
A sum of independent Poissons is Poisson with the summed mean, so Poisson(6): mean = variance = 6
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(0) − P(1) = 1 − e^(−2) − 2e^(−2) = 1 − 3e^(−2) ≈ 1 − 0.406 = 0.594.
(b) If the counts in the three separate minutes are independent, each Poisson(2), then their total is Poisson(2 + 2 + 2) = Poisson(6). A Poisson variable's mean and variance are both equal to its parameter, so the mean and variance are both 6. Even without the Poisson-sum result, linearity gives mean 6, and independence gives variance 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

questions.why: The standard deviation is √225 = 15, so z = (130 − 100)/15 = 2 and P(X > 130) = 1 − Φ(2) ≈ 0.0228. About 0.447 comes from dividing by the variance 225 instead of the standard deviation, giving z ≈ 0.133. About 0.977 is Φ(2) = P(X < 130), forgetting to take the complement. About 0.0455 is the two-tailed probability P(|Z| > 2), which double-counts for a one-sided question.

questions.q: The lifetime of a component is exponential with mean 10 years. Given that it has lasted 5 years, what is the probability that it lasts at least 10 more years?
questions.why: The rate is λ = 1/10. By the memoryless property, P(T > 15 | T > 5) = P(T > 10) = e^(−10/10) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. e^(−1.5) is the unconditional P(T > 15), ignoring the information that it has already survived 5 years. e^(−0.5) is P(T > 5), the probability of the given event, not the one asked for. 1 − e^(−1) is P(T ≤ 10), using the cdf in place of the survival function.

questions.q: X has pdf f(x) = c x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 0 otherwise. Find c, E[X], Var(X) and P(X < 1).
markScheme: ∫₀² c x² dx = 8c/3 = 1, so c = 3/8

questions.q: Var X = 4, Var Y = 9 and Cov(X, Y) = −2. What is Var(X + Y)?
questions.why: Var(X + Y) = 4 + 9 + 2(−2) = 9. 13 ignores the covariance, which is valid only for uncorrelated variables. 11 includes the covariance once instead of twice. 17 adds 2|Cov| with the wrong sign.

questions.q: X₁, …, X₁₀₀ are iid with mean 5 and variance 4, and S is their sum. Using the CLT, approximately what is P(S > 520)?
questions.why: S has mean 500 and standard deviation √(100 × 4) = 20, so P(S > 520) ≈ 1 − Φ(1) ≈ 0.159. 0.841 is Φ(1), forgetting the complement. 0.460 uses nσ = 200 as the standard deviation (scaling by n instead of √n), giving z = 0.1. 'Essentially 0' uses the standard deviation of one variable, 2, for the whole sum, giving z = 10.

questions.q: Let X ~ U(−1, 1) and Y = X². Show that Cov(X, Y) = 0 but X and Y are not independent.
markScheme: E[X] = 0 by symmetry
Cov(X, Y) = E[X³] − E[X]E[X²] = E[X³] = ∫ from −1 to 1 of x³/2 dx = 0
Find an event where the product rule fails, e.g. P(Y < ¼) = P(|X| < ½) = ½
P(Y < ¼ and X > ½) = 0 ≠ ½ × ¼, so X and Y are not independent
questions.modelAnswer: E[X] = 0 by symmetry, so Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y] = E[X³] = ∫ from −1 to 1 of x³ × ½ dx = 0, because the integrand is odd. For dependence: P(Y < ¼) = P(|X| < ½) = ½ and P(X > ½) = ¼, but the event {Y < ¼, X > ½} is impossible, so its probability is 0 ≠ ½ × ¼. So X and Y are dependent even though they are uncorrelated: covariance only detects linear association.

questions.q: Ten observations from an exponential distribution with rate λ have sum 40. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of λ?
questions.why: ℓ(λ) = n log λ − λΣxᵢ, so ℓ′ = n/λ − Σxᵢ = 0 gives λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 10/40 = 0.25. 4 is x̄, which estimates the mean 1/λ, not the rate. 0.025 is 1/Σxᵢ, dropping the n from the log-likelihood. 0.225 is (n − 1)/Σxᵢ, a different estimator (the unbiased one for λ), not the MLE.

questions.q: X₁, …, Xₙ are iid N(μ, σ²) with n ≥ 2, and σ̂² = (1/n)Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)². What is E[σ̂²]?
questions.why: E[Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²] = (n − 1)σ², because estimating μ by X̄ uses up one degree of freedom; dividing by n gives (n − 1)σ²/n. σ² would make σ̂² unbiased, which is true of S² (divisor n − 1), not of the MLE. nσ²/(n − 1) applies the correction factor upside down. σ²/n is Var(X̄), a different quantity.

questions.q: Counts x₁, …, xₙ are modelled as iid Poisson(λ). (a) Write down the log-likelihood and derive the MLE of λ, checking that it is a maximum. (b) Evaluate it for the data 2, 3, 1, 4, 0. (c) State whether the estimator is unbiased.
markScheme: ℓ(λ) = −nλ + (Σxᵢ) log λ − Σ log(xᵢ!)
ℓ′(λ) = −n + Σxᵢ/λ = 0 gives λ̂ = x̄
ℓ″(λ) = −Σxᵢ/λ² < 0 (for Σxᵢ > 0), so it is a maximum
E[X̄] = λ, so unbiased
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) L(λ) = Π e^(−λ)λ^(xᵢ)/xᵢ!, so ℓ(λ) = −nλ + (Σxᵢ) log λ − Σ log(xᵢ!). Then ℓ′(λ) = −n + Σxᵢ/λ, which is zero at λ̂ = Σxᵢ/n = x̄. Since ℓ″(λ) = −Σxᵢ/λ² < 0 whenever Σxᵢ > 0, this is a maximum. (If all xᵢ = 0, ℓ(λ) = −nλ is decreasing on λ > 0, so there is no maximum inside the parameter space; the likelihood is largest as λ → 0, in line with x̄ = 0.)
(b) Σxᵢ = 10 and n = 5, so λ̂ = 2.
(c) E[X̄] = (1/n)ΣE[Xᵢ] = λ, so the estimator is unbiased. Its variance is λ/n.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for μ is (49.9, 54.1). Which interpretation is correct?
options: The sample mean lies in the interval with probability 0.95
If the procedure were repeated on many samples, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain μ
There is a 95% probability that μ lies between 49.9 and 54.1
About 95% of the observations lie between 49.9 and 54.1
questions.why: In the frequentist framework μ is fixed and the interval is random; the 95% describes how often the method succeeds over repeated samples. Giving a 95% probability that μ lies in this particular interval treats μ as random, which needs a Bayesian analysis. The interval describes uncertainty about the mean, not where the data lie; the data are much more spread out (by roughly √n times). The sample mean is the centre of the interval, so it lies inside it with probability 1.

questions.q: In a hypothesis test, the p-value is:
options: the probability that H₀ is true
the probability of a type II error
the probability that H₁ is true
the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed
questions.why: The p-value is computed under H₀ and measures how surprising the data would be if H₀ held. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and not that H₁ is true: in the frequentist framework hypotheses have no probabilities, and those statements would reverse the conditioning. The type II error probability depends on a specific alternative and is about the test procedure, not about the observed data.

questions.q: A random sample of 16 measurements, assumed normal, has mean 52 and sample standard deviation 4. (a) Find a 95% confidence interval for μ. (b) Test H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ ≠ 50 at the 5% level. (You may use t₁₅,₀.₀₂₅ = 2.131.)
markScheme: Standard error s/√n = 4/4 = 1
T = (52 − 50)/1 = 2.0, with t₁₅ distribution under H₀
|T| = 2.0 < 2.131 (p ≈ 0.064), so do not reject H₀ at 5%
Consistent with 50 lying inside the 95% CI; conclusion stated in context
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The standard error is s/√n = 4/√16 = 1. With σ unknown, use the t distribution with 15 df: 52 ± 2.131 × 1 = (49.87, 54.13).
(b) Under H₀, T = (X̄ − 50)/(S/√16) ~ t₁₅. The observed T = 2/1 = 2.0. Since |2.0| < 2.131, we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level (two-sided p ≈ 0.064). There is only weak evidence that the mean differs from 50. This agrees with (a), because 50 lies inside the 95% interval.

questions.q: For x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, what is the least-squares slope β̂₁?
questions.why: x̄ = ȳ = 3, S_xy = 8 and S_xx = 10, so β̂₁ = 8/10 = 0.8. 1.25 is S_xx/S_xy, the formula upside down. 0.6 is the intercept β̂₀ = 3 − 0.8 × 3. 0.64 is R² = r², not the slope.

questions.q: After fitting a simple linear regression, the plot of residuals against fitted values shows a funnel: the spread grows with the fitted value, but there is no curvature. Which assumption is most clearly in doubt?
questions.why: A spread that grows with the fitted value is the signature of non-constant variance (heteroscedasticity). Problems with linearity show up as a curved trend in this plot, which is absent here. Normality is judged mainly from a QQ plot of the residuals, not from their spread against fitted values. The model makes no assumption that the intercept is zero, so it cannot be 'violated'.

questions.q: For the data x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 1, 3, 2, 5, 4: (a) find the least-squares line; (b) compute the residual sum of squares and R²; (c) given SE(β̂₁) ≈ 0.346, comment on the evidence that the slope is non-zero (t₃,₀.₀₂₅ = 3.182).
markScheme: x̄ = ȳ = 3, S_xx = 10, S_xy = 8, so β̂₁ = 0.8 and β̂₀ = 0.6
2.31 < 3.182 (p ≈ 0.10): do not reject β₁ = 0 at 5%; weak evidence with only five points
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) x̄ = ȳ = 3. Deviations of x: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; of y: −2, 0, −1, 2, 1. So S_xx = 10, S_xy = 4 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 2 = 8, and β̂₁ = 0.8, β̂₀ = 3 − 0.8 × 3 = 0.6. The line is ŷ = 0.6 + 0.8x.
(b) Fitted values 1.4, 2.2, 3.0, 3.8, 4.6 give residuals −0.4, 0.8, −1.0, 1.2, −0.6 (summing to 0). RSS = 0.16 + 0.64 + 1 + 1.44 + 0.36 = 3.6. S_yy = 4 + 0 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 10, so R² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64.
(c) t = 0.8/0.346 ≈ 2.31 on 3 df. This is below 3.182 (two-sided p ≈ 0.10), so we cannot reject H₀: β₁ = 0 at the 5% level. With only five observations, a fairly strong-looking association is still consistent with no linear relationship.

questions.q:
Let X ~ Exponential(λ), with pdf λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0, where λ > 0.
(a) Find the cdf of X, and show that E[X] = 1/λ and Var(X) = 1/λ². [6]
(b) Prove that X is memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t) for all s, t ≥ 0. [3]
(c) X₁ ~ Exp(λ₁) and X₂ ~ Exp(λ₂) are independent. Show that M = min(X₁, X₂) ~ Exp(λ₁ + λ₂). [4]
(d) S is the sum of 50 independent Exp(1) random variables. Use the central limit theorem to approximate P(S > 60), and state why the approximation is justified. [5]
(e) Explain briefly why the exact probability in (d) is a little different from your approximation. [2]
markScheme: (a) F(x) = 1 − e^(−λx) for x ≥ 0 (0 for x < 0)
(a) E[X] = 1/λ by parts; E[X²] = 2/λ², so Var = 1/λ²
(c) P(M > m) = P(X₁ > m)P(X₂ > m) by independence = e^(−(λ₁+λ₂)m)
(d) P(S > 60) ≈ 1 − Φ(1.414) ≈ 0.079; iid with finite variance, n = 50 fairly large
(e) S is skewed (it is a gamma distribution), so the normal tail is not exact; the exact value is about 0.084
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For x ≥ 0, F(x) = ∫₀ˣ λe^(−λt) dt = 1 − e^(−λx); F(x) = 0 for x < 0. By parts, E[X] = ∫₀^∞ xλe^(−λx) dx = [−xe^(−λx)]₀^∞ + ∫₀^∞ e^(−λx) dx = 1/λ. Similarly E[X²] = ∫₀^∞ x²λe^(−λx) dx = (2/λ)E[X] = 2/λ². So Var(X) = 2/λ² − 1/λ² = 1/λ².

(b) For s, t ≥ 0, {X > s + t} ⊆ {X > s}, so P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > s + t)/P(X > s) = e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs) = e^(−λt) = P(X > t).

(c) For m ≥ 0, M > m if and only if both X₁ > m and X₂ > m. By independence, P(M > m) = e^(−λ₁m)e^(−λ₂m) = e^(−(λ₁+λ₂)m). This is the survival function of Exp(λ₁ + λ₂), so M ~ Exp(λ₁ + λ₂).

(d) Each Xᵢ has mean 1 and variance 1, so E[S] = 50 and Var(S) = 50 (by independence). The Xᵢ are iid with finite, positive variance, so by the CLT, S is approximately N(50, 50). Then P(S > 60) ≈ 1 − Φ((60 − 50)/√50) = 1 − Φ(1.414) ≈ 0.079.

(e) The CLT is a limiting result. For finite n the distribution of S (which is exactly a gamma distribution with shape 50 and rate 1) is still right-skewed, so its upper tail is a little heavier than the normal one. The exact probability is about 0.084, slightly larger than the approximation.

questions.q:
The numbers of faults found on 50 independent lengths of cable are modelled as iid Poisson(λ). The total number of faults is 120.
(a) Derive the maximum likelihood estimator λ̂ and evaluate it. [5]
(b) Find E[λ̂] and Var(λ̂). [3]
(c) Use the central limit theorem to construct an approximate 95% confidence interval for λ. [4]
(d) Test H₀: λ = 2 against H₁: λ ≠ 2 at the 5% level using an approximate z-test. [5]
(e) The sample variance of the counts is 5.1. Comment on the adequacy of the Poisson model, and say how you would check it further in R. [3]
markScheme: (a) ℓ(λ) = −nλ + Σxᵢ log λ + const; ℓ′ = 0 gives λ̂ = x̄; maximum since ℓ″ < 0
(b) E[λ̂] = λ (unbiased), Var(λ̂) = λ/n
(d) |z| > 1.96: reject H₀ at 5% (borderline); conclusion in context
(e) Sample variance 5.1 is about twice the mean 2.4: overdispersion, so the Poisson model is doubtful and the CI and test are too optimistic; compare observed and fitted frequencies, plot the data
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ℓ(λ) = Σ[−λ + xᵢ log λ − log(xᵢ!)] = −nλ + (Σxᵢ) log λ − Σ log(xᵢ!). Then ℓ′(λ) = −n + Σxᵢ/λ = 0 gives λ̂ = Σxᵢ/n = X̄, and ℓ″(λ) = −Σxᵢ/λ² < 0, so this is a maximum. Here λ̂ = 120/50 = 2.4 faults per length.

(b) E[λ̂] = (1/n)ΣE[Xᵢ] = λ, so it is unbiased. By independence, Var(λ̂) = (1/n²) × nλ = λ/n.

(c) By the CLT (iid with finite variance λ), λ̂ ≈ N(λ, λ/n). Estimating the standard error by √(λ̂/n) = √(2.4/50) ≈ 0.219 gives the approximate 95% CI 2.4 ± 1.96 × 0.219 = 2.4 ± 0.429 = (1.97, 2.83).

(d) Under H₀, λ̂ ≈ N(2, 2/50), so the standard error is √0.04 = 0.2. Then z = (2.4 − 2)/0.2 = 2.0, with two-sided p = 2(1 − Φ(2)) ≈ 0.046. Since |z| > 1.96, we reject H₀ at the 5% level, but only just: there is moderate evidence that the mean fault rate exceeds 2 per length. (Using the null value λ = 2 in the standard error is natural for a test. The interval in (c) used λ̂, which is why 2 sits just inside it while the test narrowly rejects: the two approximations differ slightly.)

(e) For a Poisson model the variance equals the mean. A sample variance of 5.1 against a mean of 2.4 suggests overdispersion: faults may cluster, or lengths may differ in quality. The Poisson-based standard errors are then too small, so the interval in (c) is too narrow and the test in (d) overstates the evidence. In R I would tabulate the observed counts and compare them with the expected Poisson(2.4) frequencies (a bar chart, or a χ² goodness-of-fit test with sparse categories merged), and consider an overdispersed model.
